itineraries.title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from the glassworks of Kosta and Orrefors to Astrid Lindgren’s hometown, to Eksjö, and to the island of Visingsö.
itineraries.notes: Go between mid-June and mid-August: Astrid Lindgrens Värld, the childhood home at Näs, Kumlaby Church, and the horse-drawn carriages on Visingsö all operate daily then. You can watch glassblowing from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., daily in Kosta and Tuesday through Sunday in Orrefors.
itineraries.climate: Aim for mid-June to mid-August: in Växjö, average highs range from 20 °C in June to 22.5 °C in July, and most attractions are open daily then. July and August are also the rainiest months: bring a rain jacket, especially since umbrellas are prohibited during performances at Astrid Lindgrens Värld. Avoid winter: the park and the house at Näs are closed, and highs hover around 0 to 2 °C.

visits.text: Before watching glassblowing, it helps to understand what you are seeing. The Swedish Glass Museum, housed in the Smålands museum in Växjö, traces the country’s glassmaking from antiquity to “studio glass,” one-of-a-kind pieces that artists blow in their own studios. The Smålands museum is described as Sweden’s oldest county museum (regional museum). Admission is 150 kronor per adult and free for visitors ages 18 and under. The museum is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Start your road trip in Växjö, the most convenient gateway to the route. You can arrive by train or fly from Stockholm-Bromma: the airport is about ten kilometers northwest of town. Rent your car here, since Kosta is just a 42-minute drive away. The route ends in Jönköping: if you need to return the car in Växjö, Krösatåg regional trains connect the two cities.

practical_info.tip: Your museum ticket also includes admission to the House of Emigrants in central Växjö.

visits.text: The heat hits you as soon as you enter the glassblowing hall at Kosta Glasbruk. Furnaces have been burning in Kosta since 1742, making it Sweden’s oldest glassworks still in operation. Its name combines the first syllables of its two founders’ names, Koskull and Staël von Holstein. About 25 glassblowers work here across five workshops. You can visit the hall daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. for 70 kronor per adult: avoid 11 to 11:45 a.m., when the artisans take their break.

In 1955, Kosta expanded its showroom with a glass-walled wing designed by architect Bruno Mathsson. Look down: the floor is a glass mosaic made at the glassworks. Now the Kosta Art Gallery, the space displays art pieces by Kosta Boda’s designers. Exhibitions change two or three times a year. It is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday until 4 p.m.

Nineveh, Jerusalem, Babylon: the workers’ houses on Stora vägen, Kosta’s main street, bore the names of biblical cities. Built from the mid-18th century onward, these glassworkers’ homes were renovated in 1810 and have changed little since. Kosta’s manor house dates to 1758. Also look for Glashuset, a row of five homes designed by Bruno Mathsson, with insulating double glazing that he had patented. You can walk around the glassworks freely, at no charge.

activities.text: If you want to take home something you have blown yourself, book an introductory glassblowing session at Kosta Glasbruk. An artisan guides you step by step, and sessions start at around 500 kronor for a glass ball. In the evening, ask about hyttsill, an old glassworks tradition. You dine on herring and Småland dishes cooked in the furnaces where glass cools slowly, while watching glassblowers at work.

practical_info.tip: Public hyttsill evenings mainly take place in summer and before Christmas: check the dates on the Kingdom of Crystal website.

activities.text: Drive at walking speed in your own car among the moose at Kosta Safaripark. The park covers 200 hectares of forest, roughly the size of 280 soccer fields. Bison, red deer, and wild boar also roam freely here. Book your visit through the Kingdom of Crystal booking website: prices start at 135 kronor, with free cancellation up to 24 hours in advance.

practical_info.tip: The park is in Kosta itself, at 1 Visentvägen: there is no need to get back on the main road.

visits.text: Orrefors has lost its large glassworks, but not its glassblowers. Founded in 1898, the factory stopped production on July 12, 2013, when its owner moved manufacturing abroad. The Orranäs Glasbruk workshop later fired up furnaces on the site again. Its hall burned down in 2023, and a new octagonal hall was completed the following year. You can watch glassblowing up close Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The Orrefors museum displays the glassworks’ historical collection, from early pieces to recent creations. Before glass, Orrefors depended on iron: ironworks were established here in 1726, and the glassworks later occupied their site. In Hammarsmedjan, the restored forge, you can still hear the heavy hammer that once shaped iron into bars striking. Allow half an hour for the two, then drive to Målerås, 13 minutes away.

A highlight of the route is Målerås, a glassworks saved by its workers. Founded in 1890, it was bought in 1981 by designer Mats Jonasson and his colleagues to keep it running. Its specialty is animal reliefs engraved in crystal. The showroom and store are open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m.

activities.text: Have lunch at Målerås Glasbruk: during the high season, the restaurant has large windows overlooking the glassblowing hall. You can eat while watching molten glass take shape. The neighboring craft center sells ceramics, jewelry, wooden objects, and local products. Then allow 1 hour 36 minutes to drive to Vimmerby.

practical_info.tip: You can also book a session to blow your own piece at Målerås through the Kingdom of Crystal website.

visits.text: Astrid Lindgren was born in 1907 on Näs farm, then on the outskirts of Vimmerby. The Astrid Lindgrens Näs center was built on the very spot where she grew up, a few minutes’ walk from the main square. Its major exhibition is called “Astrid Lindgren and the Power of Stories.” Continue your visit in the gardens. In 2027, the site is open daily from May 21 to September 26.

The bed where Astrid Lindgren was born, the harmonium, a cushion she embroidered: her childhood home at Näs is still furnished as it was when she was a child. The family still owns it, and entry is by guided tour only. The tour lasts about 45 minutes, with visitors standing throughout, and is limited to 12 people ages 8 and up. English tours are also offered from May to September. Book as soon as tickets for 2027 go on sale.

Sit across from Astrid Lindgren on Stora torget, Vimmerby’s main square. Marie-Louise Ekman’s bronze statue, unveiled in 2007, shows her at her typewriter, with an empty chair opposite for visitors. Then head down Storgatan, the main street, which still follows its medieval route, and explore the cobblestone lanes around the square, including Båtsmansbacken. Astrid Lindgren is buried in the family grave in the town cemetery.

If your children could see only one setting at Astrid Lindgrens Värld, the theme park devoted to the writer’s stories, it would be Villa Villekulla. This is the home of Pippi Longstocking, whom Swedes call Pippi Långstrump. According to the park’s 2026 schedule, Pippi performed here six times a day. Bring a raincoat instead of an umbrella, as umbrellas are prohibited during performances.

Katthult was the very first house in the park, which opened in 1981 under the name Sagobyn, “the storybook village.” It is the farm where Emil lives, the mischievous boy French readers knew as Zozo la tornade. It was built at one-third of its actual size, as were all the sets built afterward, putting them on a child’s scale. Emil performed here five times a day in 2026: note the showtimes as soon as you enter, as the park covers 18 hectares.

Here, humor gives way to adventure. Mattis’s Castle provides the setting for Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter, and Cherry Valley for the story of The Brothers Lionheart. In 2026, each of these two settings hosted four shows a day. One of the park’s shows, “The Day of the Battle,” includes frightening scenes and effects. The park recommends it for ages 9 and up: check the program before settling in with young children.

activities.text: Plan your day around the shows at Astrid Lindgrens Värld: the 2026 program included 28 daily performances, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. They are performed in Swedish, so tell the children the stories before you go. In 2026, a one-day ticket in peak season cost 565 kronor per adult and 430 per child, with free admission for children under 3. The park’s stores and restaurants do not accept cash. In 2027, the park is open daily from May 21 to August 22.

practical_info.tip: After August 22, 2027, the park opens only Friday through Sunday until the end of September, then during fall break.

activities.text: The best moment of the day is not always a show. Between performances, let the children try the “Don’t Touch the Ground” trail, where they make their way along without setting foot on the ground. The Tiny Town, the play barn, and the hamlet of Bullerbyn, drawn from another series of books, round out this vast playground. There are plenty of picnic areas: securely close any bags left in your stroller, as the park’s birds help themselves.

practical_info.tip: Dogs are allowed on a short leash, but not inside buildings.

visits.text: In 1856, a fire destroyed half of Eksjö but spared the northern part of its wooden old town. This district, Gamla stan, is lined with wooden houses from the 17th and 18th centuries and has numerous courtyards. Almost the entire old town has protected heritage status. Eksjö has also received the Europa Nostra Award, a European distinction for heritage conservation. In summer, the town museum organizes guided walks.

Eksjö museum tells the story of the town’s 600-year history in the heart of the old town. The top floor is devoted to Albert Engström (1869–1940), an illustrator known for caricatures that mocked the failings of his time. Another room traces Eksjö’s military past. The town was long nicknamed the “town of hussars,” after these army cavalrymen. Then take a break in the courtyard, where an herb garden runs alongside the river.

To see how the upper classes lived in a small Swedish town in the 19th century, step inside Aschanska gården. The Aschan family, whose members included manufacturers and judges, lived here for three generations, from the 1830s until 1984. The entire interior of this upper-middle-class home has been preserved. Guided tours run daily in summer: book through Eksjö museum, which organizes them.

activities.text: Even in midsummer, the air turns cool at the bottom of Skurugata, a rocky gorge 800 m long and 7 m wide in places, 10 km northeast of Eksjö. In some years, snow and ice have lingered here into summer. Its origins are still debated: the most common explanation points to two parallel fractures in the rock. A 2 km loop starts at the parking lot, passes the Skuruhatt viewpoint, then descends into the gorge.

practical_info.tip: Wear sturdy shoes: in the gorge, you will need to step over boulders and fallen tree trunks.

visits.text: On July 11, 1897, explorer Salomon August Andrée, born in Gränna, took off from Svalbard with two companions in a hydrogen balloon, intending to fly over the North Pole. The balloon landed on the sea ice just over two days later, and the three men never returned. Their remains were found in 1930 on White Island (Kvitøya). Grenna Museum displays their belongings, photographs, and a replica of their ice shelter. In summer, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing 80 kronor per adult.

The layout of Brahegatan, Gränna’s main street, was no accident. Count Per Brahe the Younger founded the town in 1652 and aligned its streets toward his Brahehus Castle on the hill. Amalia Eriksson, who invented the local candy sticks, lived at number 2. Andrée’s birthplace is at number 37. Then climb Grännaberget, the hill above town: its open-air museum, dating from 1912, brings together historic buildings and offers free admission.

On a clear day, head up to Brahehus to see Lake Vättern and the island of Visingsö at your feet, 180 m below. Count Per Brahe the Younger had this castle built in the 17th century. A fire that spread from the neighboring village of Uppgränna destroyed it in 1708. The ruins, 3 km from Gränna, are accessible free of charge day and night, right beside a service area on the E4 highway.

activities.text: Swedes call it “polkagris,” literally “polka pig”: at the time, “gris” was a colloquial word for candy, and the polka was the fashionable dance. This red-and-white candy stick was invented in Gränna in 1859 by Amalia Eriksson. About a dozen candy shops in town make it before your eyes. The sugar is cooked to around 150 °C, then pulled: the air worked into it turns it white, and it is twisted by hand.

practical_info.tip: Some candy shops let you try twisting your own candy stick: it is not as easy as it looks.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry from Gränna to Visingsö (25 minutes)
to_next_leg.justification: Direct ferry crossing from Gränna to Visingsö, year-round, 25 minutes; the distance becomes 7 km, the straight-line distance between the two points, and the 25 minutes cover the crossing alone, with no waiting time.

visits.text: Prisoners of war are often blamed for setting fire to Visingsborg, but the tourist office tells a different story. On the evening of December 22, 1718, a sergeant named Johan Rasch burned some straw from his mattress in the stove to light his pipe. The fire broke out later. Only the south wing remains of the Brahe family’s castle, completed in 1662 after nearly a century of construction. The ruins are right next to the harbor: you can walk around them freely, but you cannot go inside the walls, which are at risk of collapse.

Climb the narrow, steep staircase in the bell tower of Kumlaby kyrka, a church dating from the early 12th century. In 1636, Per Brahe the Younger had the spire shortened to install a platform at the top for observing the stars. On a clear day, you can see four Swedish provinces from there. Inside, the wall paintings date from the 15th and 17th centuries. The church is open daily from mid-June to mid-August, and admission costs 20 kronor per adult.

The ruins of Näs, at the southern tip of Visingsö, are the remains of Sweden’s first royal castle. In the 12th century, the Sverker dynasty made it their residence, and four Swedish kings died on the island. The castle was destroyed in 1318. The tourist office recommends having a picnic there overlooking the lake: pick up a packed lunch at the harbor’s fish shop before you set off.

activities.text: Cycling is still the best way to see Visingsö: the island is 14 km long, and its narrow roads are mostly paved, with a few gravel stretches. Rent a bike at the harbor, then head south toward the oak forest. The Swedish navy began planting it in 1831 to provide timber for its warships. By the time the trees were large enough, ships were being built from other materials, and the forest remained.

practical_info.tip: If you don’t have a bike, take a remmalag, a horse-drawn carriage that leaves from the harbor: 40 minutes through the forest for 160 kronor per adult, daily from June to August.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry to Gränna (25 minutes), then E4 to Jönköping
to_next_leg.justification: Leg 1: ferry from Visingsö to Gränna, 7 km in 25 minutes; leg 2: E4 highway from Gränna to Jönköping, approximately 38 km in 31 minutes; driving is the main mode of transportation by both duration and distance.

activities.text: End the trip in Jönköping, 31 minutes from Gränna via the E4 highway. The station’s transportation hub, the resecentrum, brings together trains and intercity buses. Regional trains run to Nässjö, Växjö, and Gothenburg via Falköping. SJ trains also depart for Stockholm. Jönköping Airport has had no scheduled flights since 2020: to fly home, travel through another city.

practical_info.tip: The resecentrum also houses a bus station, with intercity buses to Stockholm, Gothenburg, and Malmö.

seo.h1_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Växjö with its glass museum, crosses the Kingdom of Crystal from Kosta to Målerås, then includes two nights in Vimmerby, Astrid Lindgren’s hometown. It continues through Eksjö’s wooden old town and Gränna, on the shores of Lake Vättern, before a morning of cycling on the island of Visingsö. The route ends at Jönköping train station.
seo.seo_hook: Glassblowers in Kosta, the house where Astrid Lindgren was born in Vimmerby, Eksjö’s wooden town, and Gränna’s candy sticks: Småland in 4 days.
featured_list: Kosta: Sweden’s oldest operating glassworks, open to visitors daily
Vimmerby: Astrid Lindgren’s childhood home and the Astrid Lindgrens Värld theme park
Eksjö: a wooden old town and the 800 m long Skurugata gorge
Gränna and Visingsö: the polkagris candy stick, invented in 1859, and Kumlaby’s bell tower observatory

itineraries.title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Karlstad to Selma Lagerlöf’s home, the lakes of Glaskogen, and the Håverud Aqueduct.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary is designed for summer: in 2026, Mårbacka, Rottneros Park, and the Dalsland Canal boats all operated from June 13 to August 22, except June 19–21, the Midsummer weekend. The boat does not depart on Sundays, so make sure your day in Håverud falls between Monday and Saturday.
itineraries.climate: Visit from mid-June to mid-August: in Karlstad, average highs reach 20 to 22 °C from June through August. Canal boats do not run on Sundays. Avoid November through March: highs stay between 0 and 5 °C, and most sites are closed or offer only a few tours.

visits.text: Ugly, perhaps, but with a fine story to tell: the woman with the broken sword on Stora torget, Karlstad’s main square, was voted “Sweden’s ugliest statue” by a television show. Fredsmonumentet, the Peace Monument, was unveiled in 1955. It commemorates the peaceful separation of Sweden and Norway in 1905. That agreement was negotiated and signed in Karlstad. Northwest of the square, also look for the statue of Sola, an 18th-century waitress nicknamed “the sun” for her cheerful disposition.

On July 2, 1865, a fire destroyed almost all of Karlstad. Only the cathedral and a few houses remained standing. Even so, Domkyrkan, the cathedral, lost its bell tower and roof that day. It had been completed in 1730 by Christian Haller, a builder from Saxony. The tower you see today was rebuilt after the fire. Then look at the layout of the surrounding streets: after the fire, the city was rebuilt on a grid, with wide, tree-lined streets.

For us, Karlstad’s most beautiful walk crosses Östra bron, the old stone bridge. At 168 m long, with twelve arches, it is Sweden’s longest stone arch bridge. Construction took fifty years, from 1761 to 1811. Legend has it that its master builder, Anders Jacobsson, took his own life for fear the bridge would collapse. That is untrue: he died at home in 1804. The bridge is about 600 m northeast of Stora torget, over the eastern branch of the Klarälven River.

If you visit just one museum in Karlstad, choose Värmlands museum, the museum of the Värmland region. It tells the region’s story from the Ice Age onward. Since 1998, a passageway has connected the oldest building, dating from 1929, to a modern wing. The museum occupies the tip of Sandgrundsudden, beside the Klarälven River. Admission costs 120 kronor and is free for visitors age 20 and under. It opens daily, staying open until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays.

Right next to the museum, the former Sandgrund dance hall, a restaurant where people used to come to dance, now houses the Sandgrund Lars Lerin gallery. It displays watercolors by Lars Lerin, born in Munkfors in 1954. The tourist office describes him as one of the Nordic countries’ leading watercolor artists. The paintings on display change about once a year. The gallery opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., with admission costing 120 kronor. In summer, its terrace overlooks the river.

activities.text: At Inre hamn, the inner harbor, board a båtbuss, a water bus on the regional transit network. Karlstad is built on the delta where the Klarälven River flows into Lake Vänern. This is the largest lake in Sweden and the European Union: 5,650 km² dotted with about 22,000 islands and rocks. Route 93 takes you to the islands of Jäverön or Västra Långholmen, depending on the day. In 2026, water buses ran from June 8 to August 30, and a one-way trip cost 33 kronor.

practical_info.tip: Check the time of the last return boat in the Värmlandstrafik app before setting out. For a shorter outing, route 92 offers a narrated city tour that must be booked in advance.

visits.text: In 1909, Selma Lagerlöf became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The following year, she used the prize money to buy back Mårbacka, the estate where she was born in 1858 and which her family had lost. Between 1921 and 1923, architect Isak Gustaf Clason enlarged the small red-painted house, turning it into a manor house. In accordance with her final wishes, the house has been preserved as it was when she died in 1940. The house can only be visited on a guided tour: 220 kronor, including admission.

activities.text: Shrubs, fruit trees, vegetable beds, and flower beds: Selma Lagerlöf created the garden at Mårbacka with horticulturist Ruth Brandberg, and the current gardener is working to restore that layout. In the 19th century, her father planted a small grove here where people would drink toddy, a hot drink made with liquor, water, and sugar. Set aside some time for the estate café, which serves homemade cakes. From June through September, admission to the garden alone costs 70 kronor.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, Mårbacka was open daily from June 13 to August 23. English-language tours, offered at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. in the height of summer, must be booked in advance; other tours are mostly in Swedish.

visits.text: The loveliest detour in the Fryken Valley is Rottneros Park, a 22 ha lakeside park filled with flowers and sculptures. Selma Lagerlöf made the estate famous as Ekeby in Gösta Berling’s Saga, her first novel, published in 1891. The old manor house burned down in 1929. Starting in 1932, miller Svante Påhlson created the park, which now holds around a hundred sculptures, including works by Swedish sculptor Carl Milles. The new manor house is private.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, leave time for the playground at Rottneros Park, named after Nils Holgersson. He is the hero of Selma Lagerlöf’s children’s book, published in 1906 and 1907: a boy who travels across Sweden on the back of a goose. The playground follows the park’s opening hours. In the height of summer, a snack stand sells light bites, with payment by card only.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the park was open from May 30 to September 6, closed on June 19, with hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., extended to 5 p.m. from June 27 to August 2. Admission: 140 kronor per adult, 50 per child. All payments are by card.

visits.text: Sundsbergs gård, an 18th-century estate near downtown Sunne, served as the model for the Björne estate in Gösta Berling’s Saga. The novel begins with a ball at Ekeby, now Rottneros, and ends here. Sunne itself appears in Selma Lagerlöf’s books as Broby. In 1893, a fire devastated the main house, and the family moved into the wing. That wing now houses the museum. The café and gallery open Wednesday through Sunday, until 4 p.m.

activities.text: Head up Tossebergsklätten, a hill north of Sunne, toward the end of the day. The narrow, steep road climbs more than 200 m in just over 2 km. At the summit, 342 m above sea level, an observation tower overlooks the Fryken Valley. You will see its long, narrow lakes. Sunne is built on the strait connecting two of them, Övre Fryken and Mellan-Fryken. The summit café opens for the season in May.

practical_info.tip: Allow time in your evening for the round trip from Sunne: the summit is about 16 km north of town as the crow flies.

visits.text: The scent of flax fills Klässbols Linneväveri, a linen weaving mill established in the village in 1920. Here you can follow the entire production process, from preparing the yarn to inspecting the finished pieces. The looms range from 19th-century handlooms to modern machines. Since 1991, the mill has supplied the linens for the Nobel banquet in Stockholm: around 500 m of tablecloth and 1,350 napkins. From May through September, the workshop and store are open daily.

activities.text: A canoe offers the best view of Glaskogen. Established in 1970, this nature reserve covers nearly 29,000 ha of forests and lakes between Arvika and Årjäng. Its name means “Gla Forest.” Its two largest lakes are Stora Gla and Övre Gla. At Lenungshammar, in the heart of the reserve, the rental center provides canoes, paddles, and life jackets. To get started, choose the easy Buvatten route, which takes 2 to 3 hours. Avoid Övre Gla in windy weather: this large lake can turn choppy in minutes.

practical_info.tip: The center does not rent canoes before May 13, in bad weather, or when the water is too cold. In midsummer, it is generally open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. To paddle or hike in the reserve, buy a Glaskogen pass at the Lenungshammar reception center; it is free for children under 16.

activities.text: Next, follow the 5 km loop trail that starts at the Lenungshammar reception center. Its first section is suitable for strollers and wheelchairs. Glaskogen has around 300 km of trails marked in orange, with wooden shelters and cabins for overnight stays. Loons, large waterbirds that dive for fish, nest near several lakes. In summer, Café Carl, right by the reception center, is a good place for a break before hitting the road.

practical_info.tip: Cell service is weak in parts of the reserve: download the map before setting out. From April 15 to September 15, fires are allowed only in designated fire pits.

visits.text: At the top of Majberget, a wooded hill in Bengtsfors, Gammelgården brings together more than 20 historic houses. This open-air museum, the largest in western Sweden, features a prosperous farmer’s homestead, a miller’s house, and a soldier’s house. A house from Nössemark, built in the 1850s, was reassembled here in 1929. The grounds are freely accessible: stroll among the houses when you arrive in the evening. In summer, guided tours sometimes provide access to the interiors for 100 kronor.

At Håverud, the Dalsland Canal had to cross a river with powerful rapids between very steep rock faces. Building conventional locks here was impossible. Engineer Nils Ericson therefore carried the canal over the river in an aqueduct: a steel-plate trough about 33 m long that spans the rapids. Boats float in this trough while the river flows beneath it. Higher still, a railroad bridge and a road bridge cross overhead. Arrive around 10 a.m. to see it before boarding the boat.

Small museum, big story: Kanalmuseet, the canal museum, has occupied the former Håverud factory office since 1971. It shows life along the Upperud River before and after the canal. Built from 1864 to 1868, the Dalsland Canal connects lakes over around 250 km. Only about 10 km had to be excavated. Its 31 locks raise boats a total of 66 m. The museum is open daily from June through August; adult admission costs 50 kronor.

Upperud Lock, close to Håverud, deserves a visit: the tourist office ranks it among the most beautiful on the canal. Its two chambers raise or lower boats by 5 m. The canal company, Dalslands Kanal AB, has its headquarters here. In summer, a former lakeside warehouse houses a small museum and a café. A ten-minute walk away, Dalslands konstmuseum, the Dalsland art museum, displays works related to nature; check its hours before visiting.

activities.text: Board at Håverud at 10:50 a.m. for the Halva Kanalrundan, the “half-canal cruise,” to Långbron. The boat passes through 10 locks, including the four consecutive locks at Håverud, which overcome an elevation difference of 9.9 m. It also crosses the aqueduct. Built in 1868, this aqueduct is held together by 33,000 rivets, none of which have needed replacing. The company operates two boats: M/S Storholmen, built in 1896, and M/S Dalslandia, which arrived on the canal in 1973. Around 2 p.m., a railcar—a small motorized train—takes you from Långbron back to Håverud.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the boats operated from June 8 to August 22, except on Sundays and over Midsummer weekend (June 19–21). Expect to pay 510 kronor, excluding the meal. Book on the Dalslands Kanaltrafik website and pick up your tickets at the boat 30 minutes before departure. Cash is preferred: cell service is weak along the canal. Parking in Håverud is free.

visits.text: The waters of Lake Vänern lap against the gates of Köpmannebro Lock, the first lock on the Dalsland Canal. It takes boats from Lake Vänern into Lake Svanefjorden. It is also the largest lock on the canal: 35.6 m long and 7.1 m wide, the same dimensions as the locks on the Göta Canal, Sweden’s other major canal. Passing through takes only about ten minutes because the difference in water levels is very small. When the lock is operating, its café sells ice cream.

activities.text: Walk from Köpmannebro to the island of Lindön: a tunnel passes beneath the railroad tracks, then a path follows the embankment. Near Lindön Lighthouse, a rocky knoll offers a view of Lake Vänern. Plants typical of limestone soils grow on the slabs of schist along the shore. The neighboring island of Långön is also accessible on foot. Mellerud station, served by SJ trains to Gothenburg and Karlstad, is about ten minutes away by car.

practical_info.tip: Allow extra time to catch your train: Mellerud is about 11 km from Köpmannebro.

seo.h1_title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Karlstad, on the shores of Lake Vänern, and heads up the Fryken Valley to Mårbacka, Selma Lagerlöf’s home, and Rottneros Park. You then paddle across the lakes of Glaskogen Nature Reserve before cruising along the Dalsland Canal to the Håverud Aqueduct, where the canal crosses above a river.
